items.prompt: What does an SLI measure?
choices: A signal close to what users experience, such as success rate
How busy one server's processor happens to be at this very moment
How many engineers are currently on the on-call rota
items.explanation: An SLI is a measured signal tied to outcomes users feel.

items.prompt: What is an SLO?
choices: A legal contract that refunds customers whenever it is missed
An internal target set on an SLI over a window of time
A dashboard panel showing a single node's disk usage
items.explanation: The SLO is the team's own target, such as 99.9% over 30 days.

items.prompt: What is an SLA?
choices: A private target the team keeps to itself and never shares
A measurement of how quickly the pages load for users
A contractual promise to customers, with consequences if missed
items.explanation: The SLA is the external commitment, usually with credits or penalties.

items.prompt: Which is normally looser, the SLO or the SLA?
choices: The SLA, which leaves the team a buffer to react in
The SLO, which leaves the customers a buffer to react in
Neither; the two are always set to the same number
items.explanation: Keeping the SLA looser means missing the SLO is a warning, not yet a breach.

items.prompt: Which is the best SLI for a checkout service?
choices: The percentage of memory used on node two
The share of checkout requests that succeed
The number of servers currently in the cluster
items.explanation: Success rate is a signal close to what a customer experiences.

items.prompt: In '99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days', which part is the SLI?
choices: The figure 99.9% taken on its own
The 30-day window length by itself
The share of requests that succeed
items.explanation: The SLI is the measured quantity; 99.9% is the target on it.

items.prompt: Why is CPU usually a poor SLI?
choices: Users can be failing while CPU still looks normal
CPU usage cannot be measured by any common monitoring tool
CPU only has any effect on users during weekends
items.explanation: CPU is an input; the failing connection pool in L1 left it normal.

items.prompt: What does an SLO turn a raw number into?
choices: A permanent record of every incident ever suffered
A decision boundary: fine on one side, act on the other
A guarantee that no request will ever fail again
items.explanation: A target gives the measurement a threshold that says when to act.

items.prompt: A team promises customers 99.9% in contract and also uses 99.9% as its internal SLO. Over a month the service reaches 99.85%. What follows?
choices: The contract is breached at the same moment the internal bar is missed, with no warning time
Only the internal target is missed, so there was time to react before any refund was owed
Neither is missed, because 99.85% rounds up to the 99.9% figure that was promised in the contract
The SLA is unaffected, because SLAs only ever cover total outages and not partial failures
items.explanation: Equal SLO and SLA means the first warning is also the worst outcome: there is no buffer.
items.reference:
Signal, target, contract
SLI: share of checkout requests that succeed
SLO: internal target, 99.9% over 30 days
SLA: external promise, 99.5%, credit if missed
SLA looser than SLO = a buffer to react in
Why: the SLI is what you measure, the SLO is what you aim for, the SLA is what you owe, and the gap between the last two gives you time.
items.learnMore:
SLI, SLO and SLA

Three terms share one number-shaped sentence. The SLI is a measurement close to user experience, the SLO is an internal target on it, and the SLA is the external contract, kept looser so that missing the SLO warns the team before money is owed.

Common mistake

Choosing an SLI because it is easy to instrument (CPU, memory) rather than because it reflects what a user experiences.
items.reflection: Think of a promise you make to yourself and a looser one you make to someone else. What does the gap between them buy you?

items.prompt: Which candidate is the best SLI for the question 'is checkout working for users?'
choices: Per-node CPU utilisation averaged across the four checkout nodes each minute
Share of checkout requests answered successfully, counted across all nodes each minute
Count of checkout nodes whose disk usage is under the alerting threshold
Number of deploys finished this week without needing a rollback to be run
items.explanation: Only the success-rate share is a direct signal of what a customer experiences; the others are inputs or process measures.

A is the SLO, B is the SLA, and C is the SLI
A is the SLI, B is the SLA, and C is the SLO
A is the SLI, B is the SLO, and C is the SLA
items.explanation: A is a measurement (SLI), B an internal target (SLO), C an external consequence (SLA).

items.prompt: An engineer proposes setting the SLO looser than the SLA to give customers extra headroom. What is wrong with that?
choices: The team could breach the contract while still meeting its own target, so nothing warns them first
Nothing is wrong: customers benefit from the headroom and the team gets a bigger error budget

It makes the SLI impossible to measure, because the target would sit above the signal itself
items.explanation: The SLO exists to trigger action before the SLA is at risk; a looser SLO means the contract breaks first.

items.prompt: What is an error budget?
choices: The money set aside for the monthly server bill
The amount of failure that an SLO allows
The number of alerts allowed to fire each week
items.explanation: A 99.9% SLO means 0.1% of the window may be bad.

items.prompt: A 99.9% SLO over 30 days allows roughly how much bad time?
choices: About 4 hours
About 4 minutes
About 43 minutes
items.explanation: 0.1% of 43,200 minutes is 43.2 minutes.

items.prompt: When does the error budget refill?
choices: When the SLO window rolls over
As soon as an incident has been resolved
Never; it can only ever shrink over time
items.explanation: The pool is per window, so it resets when the window turns over.

items.prompt: The budget is almost gone early in the window. What is the sensible move?
choices: Ship more changes faster to catch up on the work
Slow down risky changes until stability returns
Raise the SLO target in the middle of the month
items.explanation: Little budget left means little room to absorb a bad change.

items.prompt: How many minutes are in a 30-day window?
items.explanation: 30 days x 24 hours x 60 minutes = 43,200.

items.prompt: Which SLO leaves the smaller error budget?
choices: 99.99%, because it allows less failure
99%, because it allows less failure
Both leave exactly the same error budget
items.explanation: A higher target means a smaller permitted failure ratio.

items.prompt: What is the budget best understood as?
choices: A report card filled in after the month ends
A spendable allowance that informs decisions
A penalty that customers charge for outages
items.explanation: It is meant to be read before deciding how much risk to take.

items.prompt: 5 of 43.2 budget minutes have been used. How many remain?
choices: 48.2 minutes
5.0 minutes
38.2 minutes
items.explanation: 43.2 minus 5 leaves 38.2.

items.prompt: A 99.9% SLO over a 30-day window: how much bad time does the budget allow?
choices: 43.2 minutes, which is 0.1% of 43,200
4.32 minutes, which is 0.01% of 43,200
432 minutes, which is 1% of 43,200
86.4 minutes, which is 0.2% of 43,200
items.explanation: Allowed failure is 100% minus 99.9% = 0.1%, and 0.1% of 43,200 minutes is 43.2.
items.reference:
The budget in numbers
30 days = 30 x 24 x 60 = 43,200 minutes
99.9% SLO allows 0.1% of that = 43.2 minutes
5 minutes used leaves 38.2 minutes
99.99% SLO allows only 4.32 minutes
Why: the budget turns 'how risky can we be this week' from a gut feeling into a number that shrinks with every incident.
items.learnMore:
The error budget

An SLO of 99.9% over 30 days permits 0.1% of 43,200 minutes, which is 43.2 minutes. Every incident and rolled-back deploy draws that one pool down, and it refills when the window rolls over. The useful moment to read it is before a risky change, not after the month ends.

Common mistake

Treating the budget as a compliance figure reported at month end rather than a gauge to consult before deciding how much risk to take.
items.reflection: Think of any allowance you manage, such as time, money or energy. How does knowing what is left change what you agree to take on?

items.prompt: Mid-window, 30 of the 43.2 budget minutes are spent. A risky migration has a plausible 20-minute worst case. What is the best call?
choices: Run it now, since its worst case is smaller than the 30 minutes already spent
Run it now, because the budget refills the moment an incident is closed out
Raise the SLO to 99.95% first so the migration fits inside the larger budget
Postpone or shrink it, because the worst case exceeds the 13.2 minutes left
items.explanation: 13.2 minutes remain; a 20-minute worst case could breach the SLO. Raising the SLO would shrink the budget, not enlarge it.

items.prompt: Team X has a 99.9% SLO and team Y has 99.99%, both over 30 days. Which statement is right?
choices: Both budgets are 43.2 minutes, since the window length is the same
Y has about a tenth of X's budget, so the same incident hurts Y far more
Y has ten times X's budget, because a higher number means more allowance
X has about a tenth of Y's budget, because 99.9 is closer to zero
items.explanation: Y's allowed failure is 0.01% against X's 0.1%, so Y has 4.32 minutes against 43.2.

items.prompt: A director says 'we met our SLO this month, so the budget does not matter.' What is the flaw?
choices: A met SLO proves no users were ever affected, so what is left carries no information
The budget is only a figure for auditors and should not influence deploy decisions
Budgets only matter in months where the SLO was missed, never in months it was met
What remains still guides how much risk to take, and little left means caution
items.explanation: A met SLO can have almost no budget left, and that remainder is exactly what informs risk-taking.

items.prompt: A symptom-based alert fires on what?
choices: Every short CPU spike on any single node
Any change at all in disk usage
The SLI burning through the error budget
items.explanation: It watches the user-facing signal, not each input.

items.prompt: Which of these is a symptom?
choices: Checkout requests failing for users
Node memory sitting at 70 percent
Disk usage reaching 55 percent on one node
items.explanation: A symptom is something users experience.

items.prompt: Which of these is a resource metric?
choices: Share of failed checkouts
Memory use on node three
Slow page loads for users
items.explanation: Memory, CPU and disk are inputs, not outcomes.

items.prompt: What is alert fatigue?
choices: Alerts failing to send because the pager is overloaded
On-call engineers feeling tired after a long shift
Ignoring alerts because too many of them mean nothing
items.explanation: Noisy alerts teach people to mute the real ones.

items.prompt: Why did L1's resource dashboards miss the pool failure?
choices: No resource metric crossed a threshold
The dashboards were not being refreshed in time
Four nodes was too few to monitor properly
items.explanation: The failure lived in a connection pool, not in CPU, memory or disk.

items.prompt: What should a good page be?
choices: Fired as often as possible
Worth waking someone up for
A list of every metric in the system
items.explanation: Pages that rarely matter get ignored.

items.prompt: What goes wrong with alerting on every raw metric?
choices: It always arrives too late for every incident
It cannot be set up on more than one node
It misses real harm and fires on harmless spikes
items.explanation: It fails in both directions at once.

items.prompt: Why keep resource metrics at all?
choices: To diagnose the cause after a symptom alert fires
They are not needed; delete every one of them
To act as the primary page for end users
items.explanation: They explain why, once the SLI says what.

items.prompt: A CPU spike to 95% for 30 seconds is absorbed by autoscaling and no request fails. What happens under symptom-based alerting?
choices: A page fires, because CPU above 90% is itself a user-facing symptom
A ticket opens automatically, because every resource spike counts against the budget
No page, because the SLI never moved; the CPU panel stays for later diagnosis
A page fires only if the spike repeats ten times in an hour on one node
items.explanation: No request was affected, so the SLI and the budget are untouched.
items.reference:
Where the alert is attached
raw metric: node 3 memory at 70% (cause-ish, often harmless)
symptom: checkout success rate burning the budget
pool failure + normal gauges: only the symptom alert fires
CPU spike absorbed by autoscaling: no page
Why: a symptom alert pages on user harm, so it catches failures no threshold covers and ignores spikes users never felt.
items.learnMore:
Symptom-based alerting

Paging on every raw metric misses failures that never cross a resource threshold and fires on spikes that never reached a user. Attaching the page to the SLI burning the budget fixes both, and the resource panels stay available to diagnose after the page.

Common mistake

Deleting the resource dashboards. They are still the best tool for finding the cause once a symptom alert has fired.
items.reflection: Think of an alarm you stopped trusting. Was it about something you feel, or about a proxy for it?

items.prompt: One node's connection pool rejects 1 in 6 checkouts while every resource panel is normal. Which alerting design pages?
choices: A per-node CPU alert set to fire at 40 percent on all four nodes
A disk-usage alert set at 50 percent on every one of the nodes
An alert on memory growth over a rolling day for each node
An alert on checkout success rate burning the error budget
items.explanation: Only an alert on the user-facing SLI sees a failure that no resource metric shows.

The error budget refills faster because of the high frequency of alerts

items.prompt: A burn rate of 1 means what?
choices: The budget lasts exactly the whole window
The budget is gone after a single hour
No requests at all are failing right now
items.explanation: At rate 1 the budget runs out exactly at the end of the window.

items.prompt: At a burn rate of 2, how long does the budget last?
choices: Twice the length of the window
Half of the window
The whole window, as normal
items.explanation: Window length divided by the burn rate.

items.prompt: How is burn rate calculated?
choices: Allowed failure ratio divided by observed failure ratio
Observed failures minus the allowed failures
Observed failure ratio divided by allowed failure ratio
items.explanation: It compares how fast you fail with how fast you may fail.

items.prompt: For a 99.9% SLO, what is the allowed failure ratio?
items.explanation: 100% minus 99.9% is 0.1%, which is 0.001.

items.prompt: A 0.3% failure rate on a 99.9% SLO is what burn rate?
items.explanation: 0.003 divided by 0.001 is 3.

items.prompt: Why can a small amount of budget used still need a page?
choices: A small amount used always means a full outage
The budget refills itself every single hour
At a high burn rate the rest goes very quickly
items.explanation: The rate decides how soon the budget is empty.

items.prompt: At burn rate 120 on a 30-day window, the budget lasts about how long?
choices: 6 hours
6 days
60 hours
items.explanation: 720 hours divided by 120 is 6.

items.prompt: At burn rate 10 on a 30-day window, the budget lasts about how long?
choices: 7.2 hours
72 hours
300 hours
items.explanation: 720 hours divided by 10 is 72.

items.prompt: A 99.9% SLO over 30 days sees a steady 1.2% failure rate. How long until the budget is gone?
choices: 60 hours, at burn rate 12
12 hours, at burn rate 60
600 hours, at burn rate 1.2
6 hours, at burn rate 120
items.explanation: Burn rate is 0.012 / 0.001 = 12, and 720 hours / 12 = 60 hours.
items.reference:
Burn rate to time-to-empty (99.9%, 30 days)
burn rate = observed failure ratio / allowed failure ratio
0.3% failing = burn rate 3 = budget gone in 240 hours
12% failing = burn rate 120 = budget gone in 6 hours
time to empty = 720 hours / burn rate
Why: the same amount spent can be harmless at a low burn rate and urgent at a high one, because the rate decides how soon it runs out.
items.learnMore:
Burn rate

Burn rate is the observed failure ratio divided by the ratio the SLO allows. A rate of 1 spends the budget exactly over the window; 120 empties a 30-day budget in about 6 hours. Pairing a long and a short window stops pages for blips that already ended.

Common mistake

Paging on the percentage of budget used so far. It describes the past; the burn rate describes how soon the future runs out.
items.reflection: Think of something you spend steadily, such as money or attention. When is the speed of spending more worrying than the total?

items.prompt: Two services have each spent 3% of their budget. A runs at burn rate 2 and B at burn rate 80. What should happen?
choices: Page for both equally, since they have spent the same share so far
Page for A first, since a slow leak is harder to fix than a spike
Page for neither, since 3 percent is far below any sensible threshold
Page for B now; A can be looked at during working hours
items.explanation: B empties the month in 9 hours; A would last 15 days. The rate sets the urgency.

items.reflection: Think of something you spend steadily, such as money or attention. When is the speed of spending more worrying than the total?

The highest figure a competitor advertises
What users need and the platform can sustain

It never counts any incident older than a day

items.prompt: A checkout SLO is 99%. Users complain of failed purchases while the dashboard shows the SLO met. What is the best explanation?

99% is too strict, which makes the SLO read as met through rounding errors
The error budget refilled early, wiping out the failures that users reported
items.explanation: A loose target leaves a large allowance, so a lot of failure still counts as 'met'.

items.learnMore:
Choosing the SLO

Each extra nine cuts the allowance by ten and has to be paid for in redundancy, careful deploys and on-call effort. A target that is too loose hides pain; one that is too strict gets ignored or slows delivery. A rolling window also keeps a bad incident counting until it ages out.

Common mistake

Picking the number that sounds most impressive instead of the one users need and the platform can sustain.
items.reflection: Think of a standard you hold yourself to. What would it cost to make it ten times stricter, and would you still keep it?

items.explanation: An unmeetable target is exhausted constantly and loses its meaning or throttles delivery.
